newsitem.title: USA: U.S. licensee of abortion pill sued for fraud.
newsitem.headline: U.S. licensee of abortion pill sued for fraud.

text.p: A businessman who purchased the U.S. license to the controversial French abortion pill was accused in a lawsuit Thursday of using the venture as an illegal money-making scheme.

In a lawsuit filed in Los Angeles Superior Court, KCC Delaware said it invested $6 million in a company controlled by California businessman Joseph Pike under the assumption that it would own 26 percent of a company that would manufacture and distribute the abortion-inducing drug mifepristone, known in France as RU-486.
KCC, a subsidiary of Beverly Hills, Calif.-based Giant Group Ltd., claimed in its suit that Pike has sold similar stakes to other investors at the same time he was collecting money from KCC.

"As a direct and proximate result of the Pike Defendants' conduct, the Pike Defendants have received and continue to receive monies and other consideration from members of the general public who are deceived into investing in the Pike Defendants," the lawsuit said.

KCC, which is suing to protect the stake it purchased, said that after it made its investment it learned that Pike was a disbarred attorney who had pled guilty to forgery in a fraudulent real estate scheme and had been given a two-year suspended prison sentence.

The lawsuit said Pike is the principal of San Diego-based Neogen Investors LP and a group of affiliated companies, including Danco Laboratories Inc., which holds the U.S. license for mifepristone as an abortion-inducing drug, and Neogen Pharmaceuticals Inc., which holds the license for all the drug's other potential medical uses.
Phone calls made to Pike and Neogen were not returned.

The Food and Drug Administration recently ruled the drug, which induces abortion without surgery and has been used for years throughout much of Europe, was safe and effective. It is expected to approve it for use in the United States sometime next year.

But because of the widespread anti-abortion sentiment in the United States and the somtimes violent attacks directed at abortion doctors and clinics, the name of the U.S. manufacturer and distributer has been kept a secret.
The French company Roussel Uclaf, a unit of Hoechst AG, donated the U.S. patent rights for the drug to the New York-based Population Council, which in turn sublicensed the patent.
A spokeswoman for the Population Council confirmed on Thursday that Pike holds "the controling interest in the sublicense" but declined to comment if other firms were also granted similar licenses.
Giant recently sold its cement-manufacturing operations and has been looking to use the proceeds from that sale to enter a new line of business.

"We were introduced to Joseph Pike and we thought the idea of the abortion pill was of great interest from a business and social point of view," said KCC counsel Terry Christensen. "But after we signed the agreement, some startling things came out."

KCC is seeking more than $10 million in damages as well as a ruling enforcing its stake in the venture. It maintains that mifepristone has a potential to generate more than $100 million in annual sales in the United States.
